User (line 517) is the concrete swappable model (swappable='AUTH_USER_MODEL' at line 526).

AuthConfig.ready() (line 18) registers check_user_model with the system check framework (line 33). Sets default_auto_field (line 14). Entry point that wires auth into Django startup.

migration_trace: Step 1 — Audit current model: The existing model extends AbstractUser (django/contrib/auth/models.py:446). List all fields that come 'for free' from AbstractBaseUser (password:base_user.py:44, last_login:base_user.py:45) and AbstractUser (username:models.py:456, first_name:468, last_name:469, email:470, is_staff:471, is_active:476, date_joined:484). The three app-specific fields (profile_tier, external_sso_id, last_sync_at) have no counterpart and must be carried forward manually.

Step 2 — Define a custom manager: Subclass BaseUserManager (django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:21) and implement create_user() and create_superuser() that also accept/set profile_tier. Mirror the pattern in UserManager (models.py:140) but remove AbstractUser-specific defaults that no longer apply.

Step 3 — Create the new model extending AbstractBaseUser: In your app's models.py, write `class CustomUser(AbstractBaseUser, PermissionsMixin)`. Import AbstractBaseUser from django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:43 and PermissionsMixin from django/contrib/auth/models.py:317. Declare USERNAME_FIELD, REQUIRED_FIELDS (required by check_user_model at checks.py:45-55), and assign the custom manager.

Step 4 — Re-declare fields lost from AbstractUser: AbstractUser fields not in AbstractBaseUser must be explicitly re-declared: username (models.py:456), first_name (468), last_name (469), email (470), is_staff (471), is_active (476), date_joined (484). Omit any that the team no longer needs — this is the key advantage of AbstractBaseUser.

Step 5 — Carry forward the three unmappable fields verbatim: Add profile_tier = CharField(choices=[...]), external_sso_id = CharField(unique=True, null=True), last_sync_at = DateTimeField(null=True) to the new model class. No framework mapping exists for these (see unmappable_fields).

Step 6 — Wire AUTH_USER_MODEL: In settings.py, set AUTH_USER_MODEL = 'myapp.CustomUser'. The swappable hook lives at django/contrib/auth/models.py:526 (User.Meta.swappable = 'AUTH_USER_MODEL'). Django's migration framework uses this to resolve ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL) references across the project.

Step 7 — Generate and inspect migrations: Run `makemigrations`. The new migration must declare `dependencies = [('auth', '0001_initial')]` (django/contrib/auth/migrations/0001_initial.py:7) to ensure auth tables (Permission, Group) exist before the CustomUser table that references them via PermissionsMixin M2M fields (models.py:331, 342).

Step 8 — Validate with system checks: Run `manage.py check`. The check_user_model function (django/contrib/auth/checks.py:27), registered in apps.py:33, will verify USERNAME_FIELD uniqueness (checks.py:71), REQUIRED_FIELDS list type (checks.py:45), and AUTH_USER_MODEL resolution (checks.py:29). Fix any reported errors before applying migrations.

Step 9 — Write and run data migration: Create a RunPython migration that copies all rows from the old user table to the new one, including profile_tier, external_sso_id, and last_sync_at. Use apps.get_model() inside the migration function (pattern from UserManager at models.py:153) to avoid importing the live model class.

Step 10 — Update foreign keys and admin: Replace any ForeignKey/OneToOneField pointing to the old User model with settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL. Update ModelAdmin, forms, and backends. Re-register check_models_permissions errors if custom permissions are defined (checks.py:123).

unmappable_fields.reason: Neither AbstractBaseUser (django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:43-56) nor AbstractUser (django/contrib/auth/models.py:446-495) define any field for subscription tier, billing plan, or role-like categorisation. The contrib.auth design deliberately scopes the User model to authentication and authorisation state only; business-domain attributes like pricing tiers are out of scope.
unmappable_fields.migration_strategy: Retain profile_tier as a first-class field on the new AbstractBaseUser subclass. Alternatively, extract it to a one-to-one related UserProfile model (keeps the auth model lean). If using choices=['free','pro','enterprise'], add a database-level CHECK constraint via Meta.constraints for data integrity. No contrib.auth changes needed.
unmappable_fields.evidence: django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:44-45 (only password and last_login are declared); django/contrib/auth/models.py:456-484 (AbstractUser adds username/name/email/is_staff/is_active/date_joined — no tier field)

unmappable_fields.reason: contrib.auth has no SSO identifier field. The username field (models.py:456) is unique but is a human-readable handle and carries a UnicodeUsernameValidator, making it unsuitable as an opaque SSO token. The AbstractBaseUser USERNAME_FIELD contract (validated by checks.py:71) allows a custom field to be the login key, but the framework still provides no SSO-specific storage.
unmappable_fields.migration_strategy: Keep external_sso_id = CharField(unique=True, null=True, blank=True) on the new model. If SSO is the primary auth path, consider setting USERNAME_FIELD = 'external_sso_id' and defining a matching BaseUserManager.get_by_natural_key() (base_user.py:36) that looks up by this field. Add a partial unique index (WHERE external_sso_id IS NOT NULL) at the database level to enforce uniqueness only for SSO-linked accounts.
unmappable_fields.evidence: django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:36-37 (get_by_natural_key uses USERNAME_FIELD — customisable but no SSO field exists); django/contrib/auth/checks.py:71 (check enforces USERNAME_FIELD uniqueness, not SSO-specific logic)

unmappable_fields.reason: The closest built-in field is last_login (base_user.py:45), updated by the update_last_login signal receiver (models.py:16-20). However last_login tracks authentication events, not data-sync operations. There is no sync-timestamp concept anywhere in django/contrib/auth/. Conflating the two would corrupt auth audit semantics.
unmappable_fields.migration_strategy: Retain last_sync_at = DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True) on the new model. Update it via an explicit service-layer call whenever external sync occurs — do not hook into auth signals (login/logout in signals.py). If sync is frequent, consider indexing this field for queries filtering recently-synced users. The update_last_login pattern (models.py:16-20) can serve as a code template for writing a parallel update_last_sync signal.
unmappable_fields.evidence: django/contrib/auth/base_user.py:45 (last_login is the only timestamp field; it is null=True but semantically bound to auth events); django/contrib/auth/models.py:16-20 (update_last_login writes to last_login on user_logged_in signal — no equivalent sync signal exists)
